## Executive Summary

> The reference materials available for this report do not contain company-specific financial or valuation data on Wistron (3231.TW); the passages instead cover broader Taiwan macro trade data, semiconductor supply-chain commentary, and other individual ODM/component names.

This backdrop is broadly relevant to Taiwan-based ODM/EMS players such as Wistron, which sit within the same electronics export supply chain, though no order or revenue figures specific to the company are available in the provided materials. Separately, sector commentary on AI server-related demand highlights continued strength in server platform build-outs and value-content upgrades across the supply chain — for example, BMC/management-chip suppliers are seeing new product ramps tied to multi-node, multi-card AI server architectures expected to scale through 2026–2027 [2], and other ODM peers are expanding AI server production capacity with meaningful revenue contribution targeted for the second half of 2026 [3]. These trends are consistent with a generally constructive demand environment for AI server assembly and related hardware, a segment relevant to Wistron's business exposure, but they should be 2026F total server shipment 1Q26 white-box/ODM server growth shipment growth read as industry context rather than company-specific guidance. Given the absence of Wistron-specific revenue, margin, valuation, or rating data in the source materials, no numerical outlook (EPS, target price, rating) can be responsibly presented here.

A definitive investment view on Wistron 3231 would require company-level financial statements, order visibility, and broker valuation inputs beyond what is available in this reference set. Custom-built ("white-box") servers, the segment where large ODM assemblers such as Wistron and its listed affiliate Wiwynn compete most directly, are outgrowing the branded server market: 1Q26 white-box ODM shipments rose 53% y/y versus only 2% for branded servers, lifting the white-box share of total shipments to roughly 40% in 1Q26 [13].

### Mix Shift Toward White-Box and ODM Assembly

```chart
{"type": "bar", "title": "Global Server Shipments, 2020-2027F", "source": "[13]", "x": ["2020", "2021", "2022", "2023", "2024", "2025", "2026F", "2027F"], "series": [{"name": "Units (mn)", "values": [12.7, 12.9, 14.0, 11.4, 12.5, 13.5, 15.5, 16.7]}]}
```

**Mix shift favors white-box/ODM assembly.** Rising AI-server penetration has also pushed average server ASPs higher — the industry-wide average reached US$31,000 in 2025 versus US$53,000 for CSP-specification units, with further increases expected in 2026 — implying a richer revenue pool per unit for assemblers even before unit growth is considered [13]. On the customer side, GPU and ASIC platforms are both scaling: KGI's tracker shows Nvidia GPU shipments rising from 3.84 million units (2024) to an estimated 8.24 million (2026F), alongside rapid growth in CSP-designed ASICs (Google, AWS, Meta, Microsoft), with the top five CSPs expected to account for over 70% of GB/VR-class shipments in 2026 [13]. This diversification across chip platforms — plus AMD's MI455X-based Helios rack architecture, slated to begin shipping in 4Q26 with 2027 deployments estimated at 6,000-10,000 racks — broadens the addressable rack-assembly opportunity beyond a single GPU vendor, and industry data identifies Wiwynn as a primary system integrator for one of the large hyperscale customers on this platform [17]. Separately, Digitimes/KGI shipment-share data for AI server customers (e.g., Amazon, Super Micro) list Wistron among the group of ODM suppliers (alongside Inventec, Wiwynn, Foxconn, Quanta and MiTAC) participating in this build-out, though the precise share split across vendors in that dataset is not fully resolved [13].

**Rack-level content growth from liquid cooling.** Rack-level content growth from liquid cooling. 16.7 As rack thermal design power (TDP) continues to 15.5 climb, liquid cooling has moved from an optional feature to a standard requirement for most AI server racks, expanding the addressable component value both inside and outside the rack. Nvidia's upcoming VR NVL72 platform adopts a fully modular, fanless, direct-to-chip liquid-cooling design, and KGI 2026F 2027F estimates the value of cold plates and internal manifolds in a VR200 rack will rise more than 30% versus the prior-generation GB300; 2-4MW in-row CDUs and 100-350kW sidecar units are being upgraded in parallel to support higher-density racks [17]. This shift raises the bill-of-materials value captured per rack for system assemblers, a structural tailwind for ODM revenue per unit even if rack unit growth moderates. The AI server build-out is colliding with a structural memory shortage: HBM production is being prioritized by the three major DRAM makers because of superior margins, pushing HBM capacity bookings out to 2027, while a single HBM wafer displaces roughly three DDR5 wafers in fab capacity terms [18].

**Memory supply is the key bottleneck to watch.** As AI workloads shift from training to inference, pressure extends beyond HBM to conventional DDR5, since a single AI server can require 1TB-2TB of DDR5 for KV-cache and long-context support, creating simultaneous supply displacement and demand surges for system memory [18]. New capacity requires 2-3 years to come online because bottlenecks sit in TSV advanced packaging and high-frequency process tooling rather than raw wafer supply, implying the shortage — and associated DRAM price inflation — persists through 2026 into 2027, with balanced supply-demand not expected until 2027H2-2028 [18]. Separately, memory makers are reported to prioritize HBM supply stability because any HBM shortfall would constrain GPU output, AI server shipments and, in turn, RDIMM demand — a chain of dependency that directly affects the components ODMs like Wistron must source and price into system builds [19]. Morgan is cited as raising its 2026-2028 global memory market size estimate by 37%-53%, with AI-related memory revenue rising from 6% of the total memory market in 2023 to 31% in 2025 and a projected majority share by 2028 [20].

> The central risk to the Wistron thesis is timing risk in the AI server product cycle — transitions between platform generations have already caused visible revenue air-pockets. [27] [15]

On the downside, Goldman Sachs' key risks to its Buy thesis on Wistron include a weaker-than-expected PC market recovery, a slower-than-expected ramp in AI server demand, and softer-than-expected demand for general-purpose servers [27]. Morgan Stanley's risk framework for Wistron similarly lists weaker notebook demand, softer Apple Watch-related demand, margin pressure from rising labor costs and sales shortfalls, fierce price competition in the mega data center segment, and slower-than-expected AI server penetration as the principal downside scenarios; upside risks mirror these — stronger NB and server demand and faster AI server penetration [28]. A recurring theme in the evidence is that Wistron's near-term results are sensitive to product-cycle transition timing. Reports have noted that rack-level AI server shipments were previously slowed by a model transition, with the next generation of rack-level platforms only ramping later in the year [27].

More recently, coverage points to continued topline acceleration from AI servers, with upside driven by AI racks tied to Neo Clouds/AI Natives, the start of CPU and Rubin racks beginning in Q4, growth in servers/networking off a low base, and ongoing qualification work for new customers on VR200 — Latest 0.98 Peer P/ all of which remain execution items to monitor Quarterly E vs EPS rather than confirmed outcomes [15].
